content: The Joint Commission is a private, non-profit organization based in the United States. It is one of the most prominent healthcare accreditation bodies in the country. Its stated mission is to enhance the safety and quality of care provided to the public by offering healthcare accreditation and related services that support performance improvement in healthcare organizations. Despite common misconceptions, the Joint Commission is not a governmental or global public authority. This misunderstanding arises because hospitals accredited by the Joint Commission are deemed to meet the Medicare Conditions of Participation under U.S. law (42 U.S.C. §§ 1395bb(a),(b)), which is a requirement for Medicare reimbursement. This deeming authority gives the Joint Commission significant influence, effectively making it a near-monopoly in the U.S. healthcare accreditation market. The organization generates approximately $113 million annually, primarily from fees charged to hospitals for compliance evaluations. The origins of the Joint Commission trace back to the efforts of Dr. Ernest Codman, who advocated for hospital reform through outcomes-based patient care management. His work led to the establishment of the American College of Surgeons and its Hospital Standardization Program. In 1951, the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Hospitals (JCAH) was formed by merging this program with similar initiatives from the American College of Physicians, the American Hospital Association, the American Medical Association, and the Canadian Medical Association. In 1981, the organization was rebranded as the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO), commonly pronounced jay-co. Today, it is simply referred to as the Joint Commission. In 1997, the organization launched an international branch, Joint Commission International (JCI), which accredits hospitals outside the U.S. using a distinct set of standards. The Joint Commission conducts hospital surveys to assess compliance with its standards, but the detailed findings of these surveys are not made public. However, the accreditation decision, the date of accreditation, and any cited areas for improvement are available on the organization's Quality Report, accessible through the Quality Check™ website. Hospitals that meet most or all applicable standards are granted accreditation. In the U.S., accreditation by the Joint Commission is highly sought after because it signifies compliance with Medicare and Medicaid certification requirements, which are essential for reimbursement from these programs. Historically, the Joint Commission faced criticism for its practice of notifying hospitals in advance of inspections, which allowed facilities to prepare and potentially mask ongoing issues. Reports from the Washington Post and the Boston Globe highlighted concerns about the validity of the Commission's evaluations, noting that nearly all inspected hospitals received accreditation, even when serious care delivery problems were present. In response, the Joint Commission implemented unannounced surveys for U.S. However, JCI surveys for international hospitals are still scheduled in advance, often after significant preparation by the facilities. The Joint Commission and JCI employ full-time salaried surveyors, many of whom have prior experience in healthcare services. These surveyors evaluate the operational practices and facilities of healthcare organizations, focusing on structural, input, and process metrics. They do not assess the performance of individual physicians or address medical ethical issues, as the Joint Commission ceased providing ethical guidance to U.S. hospitals years ago. The standards used for accreditation differ between the U.S. and international hospitals. JCI applies a uniform set of standards globally, without regional adaptations. While the Joint Commission holds significant influence, it is not the sole accreditation body in the U.S. In California, the Joint Commission participates in a joint survey process with state authorities. Other U.S.-based accreditation organizations include the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF), the Community Health Accreditation Program (CHAP), the Accreditation Commission for Health Care, Inc. (ACHC), the Compliance Team's Exemplary Provider Program, and the Healthcare Quality Association on Accreditation (HQAA). These organizations operate independently of the Joint Commission and are recognized in specific states, such as Ohio. The Joint Commission's mission is to continuously improve the safety and quality of care through accreditation and related services. It updates its standards and patient safety goals annually, making them publicly available on its website. The National Patient Safety Goals aim to address problematic areas in healthcare and propose evidence-based solutions, focusing on system-wide improvements. The organization's power largely stems from its role in determining hospitals' eligibility for Medicare and Medicaid participation, which compels most U.S. hospitals to seek its accreditation. The Joint Commission actively monitors state legislative and regulatory activities to identify opportunities for expanding its influence. Internationally, the demand for healthcare accreditation has grown with the rise of medical tourism. JCI accredits hospitals in regions such as Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and South America, generating revenue for its U.S.-based parent organization. JCI also offers educational programs, including Practicums, which provide training and resources for hospitals seeking accreditation. Other international accreditation bodies include the Canadian Council on Health Services Accreditation (CCHSA), the Trent Accreditation Scheme (TAS) in the United Kingdom, the Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS), and the Society for International Healthcare Accreditation (SOFIHA), which facilitates discussions and the exchange of best practices among accreditation providers and users. The costs of JCI accreditation include survey fees, travel expenses for surveyors, and additional costs for consultancy services aimed at helping hospitals prepare for the accreditation process.
